content: Hi all, been working on a formalization of O'Donnell's Analysis of Boolean functions located here: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/analysis-of-boolean-functions. The first chapter PR got merged recently after a lot of back and forth and review and I think its in pretty good shape at the moment, so I figured it is a good time to mention it here before it grows too much more.
Curious if folks feel like cslib is the right home for this work.
Boolean fourier analysis is pretty niche. But I like the idea of formalizing the book itself and putting it in a separate folder under foundations.
Yeah, I'd be happy to make a PR if that is desired. It might end up being useful for circuit complexity work down the line.

@Samuel Schlesinger Are you considering adding open problems from this book to the
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures?
No I haven't thought about that, so far I have been working on my own personal pile of conjectures here: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/open-conjecture-formalizations

It would be nice if there were a standardized way of marking something as an open conjecture in your library, and when it gets uploaded to reservoir it gets added automatically to some index of open conjecture.

So from the discussion so far, it seems like a PR with the first chapter's contents might be appreciated. However, its quite a lot of code for a single PR. Wondering if I should do it in smaller batches.
Finally getting around to making this patch. Finding lots of refactors to my original code along the way, but I should have it up within the week.

Just seeing this, I personally find it pretty interesting and in scope!

Glad you are interested! I like this book quite a lot, it might be my favorite combinatorics book.
Ryan put a copy on arxiv, pleasantly: https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10386
@Chris Henson can you move this thread into Cslib? Realizing this is why I can never find it :)
This topic was moved here from #computer science > Analysis of Boolean Functions by Chris Henson.

Also, I realized that AddChar is already in Mathlib so I'm exploring defining this stuff in terms of that. Then we can maybe just implement cs-flavored theorems into Cslib instead of doing al of the underlying maths which is done at least to some extent in Mathlib
Nah, it didn’t really work out to save anything here. I feel like it’s better to keep it self-contained.
Perhaps a bridge to AddChar would be a nice touch though.

I made a comment on the PR, but I want to bring it up here in case the maintainers don’t see that one. I think this entire PR can be developed for (finite?) abelian groups instead of ZMod 2. The book is written with a typical theory grad student in mind, who might not necessarily come from a math background.
Indeed, that is the point of the above discussion.
And Mathlib already has much of the relevant material, so a reasonable question might be whether we could simply do the theorems which are more “computer science-y” in Cslib.
It doesn’t help that PR much, but perhaps that PR instead should just be things like BLR using the stuff already in Mathlib and skipping some of the exposition in O’Donnell.
I'm no expert in this material, but it seems that O'Donnell talks about general abelian groups in sec.8.5 of his book.
Yeah, he does, but he brings it up fairly late after setting up all the theory for ZMod 2. It's a book written to teach the topic and it does this very well.
That's just pedagogy. As you said, he probably can't assume his students have the necessary mathematical background.

Exactly. From a library building perspective aiming for the higher generality is the neater route.

@Samuel Schlesinger : I would be surprised if the probabilistic interpretation is already in mathlib fwiw

On the one hand, it seems to me that the library can always be refactored later when more powerful tools and more general results are added. On the other hand, given what's already there under Mathlib.Analysis.Fourier, I think it is perhaps worthwhile to consult an expert to see whether O'Donnell's chapter 1 is an easy special case of what's already in Mathlib.
The definition of the boolean fourier transform is.
Where?
See the link in my comment from Laci Babai's notes.
Further the BLR test is, in full generality, an abelian group homomorphism test.
I'd appreciate a link.

https://www.math.toronto.edu/swastik/courses/combinatorialmethods-S23/scribe/lec8.pdf

https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/PDF/pt-lin.pdf
https://cs-people.bu.edu/sofya/pubs/TestingLinearityEncyclopedia.pdf
This is fairly basic property testing material fwiw. You'd find plenty of links with a google search. Especially the BLR test which is something typically introduced in the first one or two lectures.

Basically chapter 1 can be formalised in abelian groups. I am not sure about chapter 2, since that deals with Arrow's impossibility theorem. There's a layer of definitions from voting theory that need to be "mapped" to the corresponding boolean functions. As I recall, some of the definitions there like majority functions are defined specifically for 2 element sets. It also requires probability theory machinery that afaik will need some careful checking before it is generalised. But one can always specialise the affine group definitions for such cases as Samuel says.

(Incidentally this is the chapter I lectured on, in my first ever reading group talk nearly 9 years ago in Oxford, so I have some fond memories of it).

I took a closer look at the documents that @Shreyas Srinivas pointed out and Mathlib.Analysis.Fourier.FiniteAbelian. It seems to me that the usual formulation of Fourier analysis on finite abelian groups uses complex-valued characters, while O'Donnell's chapter 1 is formulated entirely in terms of real numbers. In fact, I think complex numbers are not used in O'Donnell's book until chapter 8 when he starts to treat general finite abelian groups. If the goal is to formalize O'Donnell's book, I'm not sure taking the more general POV of finite abelian groups is going to be very helpful (at least until chapter 8).

If you look at it closely, you'll see that there is really nothing "Fourier" in O'Donnell's chapter 1. He just proves that the parity functions forms an orthonormal basis and defines the "Fourier expansion" as the normal expansion of a vector in this basis. The Parseval and Plancherel theorems are then standard results for inner-product spaces in linear algebra. Perhaps there is a special connection between the parity functions and the Fourier analysis on abelian groups (ℤ / 2)^n. But if there is one, then that fact either is not used in O'Donnell's book or is peripheral to the results he wants to prove.

On the other hand, since I'm no expert in this area, I still think it is a good idea to consult an expert.

“If you look at it closely…” => that’s literally just Fourier transform on Z/2Z. Those complex numbers you see are roots of unity. In the case of Z/2Z, the dual group is simply {-1, 1} with complex multiplication which is why you don’t explicitly see complex numbers.
@Ching-Tsun Chou : I’d really like to hear your understanding of the definition of Fourier transforms if you seriously believe there is “nothing Fourier” going on.

Yeah, Shreyas is right here that this is indeed the Fourier transform on Z/2Z. Formalizing this textbook standalone, it makes sense to do things as I have, but moving into CSLib which is in dialogue with Mathlib it may make sense to do things over arbitrary finite Abelian groups. I still tend to think it makes sense to formalize specifically this book, but after sleeping on it we should probably use the underlying work that already exists in Mathlib and just extract the real part in this early case. In the literature, people use both the general version and the specific version and they tend to cite this book, so we should just provide both with the goal in mind to support formalization of current day cs theory work.

Samuel Schlesinger said:

so we should just provide both with the goal in mind to support formalization of current day cs theory work.

I don't understand this bit, is there something difficult about specializing out of what is already in Mathlib as needed?
Nope, I didn’t make it clear but I am leaning towards this now after sleeping on it.

The outstanding question is whether to specialize the stuff in Mathlib to implement the book as written, or to compose an interface ourselves which we think is more well-suited to current day formalization work. I believe this is Shreyas’ argument. The former has the benefit of already having a roadmap for us from an expert, the latter is probably more work that I don’t really have the bandwidth for personally, but perhaps it yields better results for users and maintainers down the line. However, if people are using and citing bits from the early parts of the book as written, we should provide this for them.

We are still in the early scenario where we don’t have a lot of users actually using this in anger to formalize their papers, so it is hard to guess how folks will want to use any of this.

For the purposes of what is upstreamed to CSLib from your repo, I don't think there is a good argument for adding a special case of what already exists in Mathlib. However, I think you should take careful note of anything missing from Mathlib and should PR this, and we likely discover through this any usability constraints.

I am fully aware that the two roots of unity of degree 2 are 1 and -1, both of which are real numbers. But the theory of characters is usually formulated over a vector space with complex scalars, where the inner product is the hermitian inner product which may produce a non-real complex number. So, at the very least, the Plancherel's theorem in O'Donnell's book doesn't seem to follow immediately from the Plancherel's theorem in the usual, complex-valued formulation. More broadly, I'm not sure how easy it is to convert results stated in terms of a complex inner-product space (the usual theory of characters) to those stated in terms of a real inner-product space (the approach taken by O'Donnell's chapter 1). That's part of the reason why I think a real expert should be consulted.

Let me spell out more details: If you want to apply the general theory of Fourier analysis on finite abelian groups to O'Donnell's chapter 1, it seems to me that you'll encounter at least the following difficulties:
(1) You need to prove that the characters on the group (ℤ / 2)^n are exactly the parity functions, which is not immediately obvious.
(2) The general theory will give you a vector space with complex scalars in which the characters form an orthonormal basis. The Fourier expansion is the expansion of a vector in this basis, but here the coefficient may be complex numbers, which is not O'Donnell's formulation of a Fourier expansion.
(3) The inner product in this vector space is the hermintian inner-product which may return a complex number. So its version of the Plancherel theorem is not exactly the version in O'Donnell's book.
Perhaps all of the above difficulties can be overcome, but that requires careful work. It seems doubtful that that work will have much to do with formalizing the results in O'Donnell's book, for he manages to carry on for at least 7 chapters without using the complex numbers at all.

Ryan responded to me via an email asking his perspective, here is his message:

To chime in briefly, I actually feel the generalization that is much much more in the spirit of the book is the generalization to functions on product probability spaces, which is set up in Chapters 8.1 and 8.3. (Here, the range would almost always be most usually R, but one could take it to be a Banach space too, as in 8.33.)

I think the case where the product components are (abelian) groups is actually not as important in the book (albeit, it does come up a decent amount in chapter 1).
